extra_misconceptions.fact: United States Mint presses strike solid, cold metal planchets under high pressure between hardened steel dies to create coins.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Molten metal is poured directly into coin-shaped molds at United States Mint facilities to form circulating coins.

extra_misconceptions.fact: A blank only becomes a planchet after it is softened in an annealing furnace and given a raised rim in an upsetting mill.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: A coin blank and a planchet are identical terms for the flat metal disk punched directly out of a coiled metal strip.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Only the Philadelphia, Denver, San Francisco, and West Point facilities strike coins; Fort Knox only stores precious metal bullion.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: The Fort Knox Bullion Depository and Washington headquarters actively strike circulating coins alongside Denver and Philadelphia.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Circulating United States coins that lack a mint mark letter were struck at the Philadelphia Mint, such as pre-1980 cents.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Coins without a visible mint mark letter were struck at the West Point facility for general everyday circulation.

extra_socratic_questions: What happens to a punched metal blank when it passes through the upsetting mill before reaching the coining press?
Which physical indicator on a circulating coin reveals whether it was struck at the Philadelphia or Denver facility?
Under what condition does a rigid metal blank crack during striking if the annealing furnace step is omitted?
What distinguishes the primary production role of the San Francisco and West Point mints from Philadelphia and Denver?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Lincoln cents and Jefferson nickels have plain, smooth edges; reeding appears on dimes, quarters, and half dollars.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: All circulating United States coins feature reeding grooves around their outer edges to prevent counterfeit production.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Clad coins are bonded from three solid metal layers with an outer copper-nickel alloy rolled onto a pure copper core.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Modern clad dimes and quarters are manufactured by dipping a solid copper coin into a thin bath of liquid silver.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Collecting one example of each major design is a type set, whereas a date set includes every year a series was struck.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: A complete date set requires collecting only one single example of each major coin design across a denomination's history.

extra_misconceptions.fact: The obverse is the front or heads side bearing the portrait, while the reverse is the back or tails side of the coin.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: The reverse of a United States coin is always the side bearing the primary portrait bust and the year of minting.

extra_socratic_questions: Which physical indicator along the edge of a quarter reveals that it is a three-layer clad coin rather than solid silver?
What distinguishes a numismatic type set of United States nickels from a date set of Jefferson nickels in a collection log?
Why were vertical reeding grooves originally added to the outer edge of higher-denomination coins during the minting strike?
Where on a coin do the mint mark and statutory mottoes help confirm which side is the obverse versus the reverse?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Soft PVC plastic releases acidic chemical plasticizers over time that coat coins in sticky green slime and corrode metal.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Soft, flexible PVC plastic flips are the safest long-term archival holders because they cushion coins against scratches.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Cardboard folders glue a backing behind the slots that hides one side of each coin and leaves the front exposed to air.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Standard tri-fold cardboard coin folders let you view both the obverse and reverse of every coin while keeping out air.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Abrasive cleaning scratches microscopic lines into a coin's original mint surface and permanently reduces its collector value.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Scrubbing tarnished or dirty coins with household baking soda or metal polish before storage restores their numismatic value.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Professional grading slabs offer tamper-evident protection and authentication, but they cost far more than folders or 2x2 holders.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Third-party hard plastic grading slabs are the least expensive storage option for organizing everyday pocket-change finds.

extra_socratic_questions: What happens to the surface of a copper or silver coin stored for years inside a soft polyvinyl chloride plastic flip?
Which storage method allows a collector to inspect both the obverse and reverse of a coin without touching its bare metal?
Under what condition can pushing a high-grade uncirculated coin into a tight cardboard folder slot damage its surface luster?
Why is it dangerous to hold a coin flat across its obverse and reverse faces with bare fingers when placing it into a holder?

extra_misconceptions.fact: The VDB initials returned to the Lincoln cent in 1918 and sit in tiny raised letters on the bottom truncation of Lincoln's shoulder.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Victor David Brenner's VDB initials were permanently removed from all Lincoln cents after the 1909 reverse controversy.

extra_misconceptions.fact: In mid-1982, the Mint switched the cent's composition from 95 percent copper bronze to a 97.5 percent zinc core plated with copper.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Lincoln cents struck from 1959 through 2008 are made of the exact same solid bronze alloy across that entire date span.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Lyndall Bass designed and Joseph Menna sculpted the 2010 Union Shield reverse, replacing Frank Gasparro's 1959 Lincoln Memorial.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: The Union Shield reverse introduced on the one-cent coin in 2010 was designed by Frank Gasparro alongside the Memorial.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Since 1999, circulating commemorative quarters place the mint mark on the obverse right behind George Washington's hair ribbon.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: State Quarters and America the Beautiful quarters still place their P or D mint mark on the reverse beneath the eagle.

extra_socratic_questions: Where should a Scout position a magnifying loupe on a Lincoln cent obverse to locate Victor David Brenner's VDB initials?
What design change occurred on the reverse of the Lincoln cent in 2010 to represent President Lincoln's preservation of the Union?
Which physical location on a 1959 to 2008 Lincoln Memorial cent displays Frank Gasparro's FG initials on the reverse?
Where did the mint mark move on United States quarters beginning in 1999 to make room for commemorative reverse designs?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Every quarter, half dollar, and dollar struck during both 1975 and 1976 carried the dual date 1776-1976 on the obverse.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Quarters, half dollars, and dollars dated 1975 are ultra-rare mint errors because almost none escaped into circulation.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Circulating Bicentennial coins use standard copper-nickel clad metal, while only special San Francisco sets contain 40 percent silver.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: All 1776-1976 Bicentennial coins are struck in 90 percent silver because they are special commemorative issues.

extra_misconceptions.fact: The Liberty Bell superimposed over the Moon is on the Eisenhower dollar, while the Kennedy half dollar shows Independence Hall.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: The Liberty Bell and Moon design appears on the reverse of the 1776-1976 Kennedy Bicentennial half dollar.

extra_misconceptions.fact: The Treasury selected the Colonial Drummer, Independence Hall, and Liberty Bell and Moon designs through an open public competition.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: United States Mint staff engravers created the three Bicentennial reverse designs internally without public participation.

extra_socratic_questions: Why are there no circulating United States quarters, half dollars, or dollar coins bearing a single 1975 obverse date?
Which three patriotic motifs were selected by national competition for the 1976 Bicentennial quarter, half dollar, and dollar?
What distinguishes the Type I and Type II reverses of the 1776-1976 Eisenhower Bicentennial dollar when logging a collection?
Where on a 1776-1976 quarter, half dollar, and dollar can you find the initials of Jack Ahr, Seth Huntington, and Dennis Williams?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Alexander Hamilton on the $10 note and Benjamin Franklin on the $100 note were Founding Fathers who never served as president.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Every portrait on current United States Federal Reserve paper currency depicts a former President of the United States.

extra_misconceptions.fact: The Bureau of Engraving and Printing produces all paper currency at its two facilities in Washington, D.C. and Fort Worth, Texas.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: United States paper currency is printed at the Philadelphia and Denver facilities alongside circulating metal coinage.

extra_misconceptions.fact: The $2 Federal Reserve note depicting Thomas Jefferson remains active legal tender and is still printed periodically by the BEP.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: The two-dollar bill featuring Thomas Jefferson was permanently discontinued and is no longer legal tender in circulation.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Currency stock is a specialized textile blend of 75 percent cotton and 25 percent linen embedded with red and blue security fibers.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: United States paper bills are printed on ordinary wood-pulp paper coated with a clear water-resistant plastic varnish.

extra_socratic_questions: Which two current United States paper currency denominations feature statesmen who never served as President of the United States?
What distinguishes the mission of the Bureau of Engraving and Printing from the United States Mint regarding paper notes?
Which physical indicator on a current Federal Reserve note reveals whether it was printed in Washington, D.C. or Fort Worth, Texas?
What security features on a current $100 note allow you to verify its authenticity by tilting the bill or holding it to light?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Tokens and medals are exonumia without statutory legal tender status, whereas coins are government-issued money with fixed face value.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Commemorative medals and transit tokens can be spent at face value in banks just like government-issued legal tender coins.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Countries inscribe coins in their own official scripts and languages, such as Nippon in kanji on Japanese coins or Helvetia on Swiss coins.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Every nation stamps its country name in English on the obverse of its circulating coinage for international identification.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Requirement 7a requires twenty different world coins spanning at least seven distinct issuing countries, each logged by design.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Collecting twenty 1-euro coins with the exact same national side completes the seven-country world coin requirement.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Polymer banknotes are moisture-resistant, harder to tear than paper bills, and incorporate clear window security features.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: World banknotes printed on polymer plastic will melt or dissolve if they accidentally get wet in humid storage conditions.

extra_socratic_questions: Which reference features help you identify a world coin's country of origin when its inscriptions use a non-Latin alphabet?
What distinguishes a privately issued transit or arcade token from a government-struck legal tender world coin?
What details should you record in your collection log when cataloging 20 world coins or banknotes from seven countries?
Why do many modern world banknotes use polymer plastic substrates with transparent windows instead of cotton-fiber paper?
